questions.enonce_markdown: (a) Account for the rejection of Esau as a Patriarch. [9 marks]
questions.corrige_markdown:
Esau, the elder twin of Isaac and Rebekah, was not chosen to carry the covenant line; Jacob was. The Genesis account gives several reasons.

1. **He despised his birthright.** In Genesis 25 Esau came in hungry from the field and sold his birthright to Jacob for a meal of lentil stew. The narrator comments that Esau "despised" his birthright. For a patriarch, the birthright carried leadership of the family, a double portion of the inheritance and a special religious role, so selling it showed that he did not value the covenant responsibility.
2. **He lacked spiritual concern and self-control.** He acted on appetite and the moment ("I am about to die, of what use is a birthright to me?"), a mark of a man unfit to preserve the promise.
3. **His marriages displeased his parents.** Genesis 26 reports that Esau married Hittite (Canaanite) women, who made life bitter for Isaac and Rebekah. The patriarchs avoided marriage with the local peoples in order to protect their faith, so this was a serious fault.
4. **God's prior choice.** Before the twins were born, Rebekah received an oracle that "the elder shall serve the younger" (Genesis 25). In the narrative the covenant line follows God's choice and not the customary right of the firstborn.
5. **The blessing passed to Jacob.** In Genesis 27, by Rebekah's plan and Jacob's deception, Isaac blessed Jacob. Whatever the moral problems of the method, the narrative holds that the blessing could not be recalled, and Esau became the ancestor of Edom, a separate people.

**Conclusion.** Esau was rejected because of his own attitude to the birthright and the covenant, his marriages and, above all, the choice of God, which the story presents as sovereign and prior to the deeds of the twins.

questions.enonce_markdown: (b) Give reasons for the call of Jacob as a Patriarch? [16 marks]
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Jacob, the younger son of Isaac and Rebekah, became the third patriarch and was renamed Israel; his twelve sons became the ancestors of the twelve tribes. The Genesis narrative gives several reasons for his call.

**1. The free choice of God.** Before birth Jacob was marked out by an oracle given to Rebekah: "the elder shall serve the younger" (Genesis 25). The biblical writers present Jacob as chosen by grace and not because of his merits. God, who calls whom he wishes, chose the younger son to show that the covenant depends on his purpose and not on human custom.

**2. The continuation of the covenant.** God had promised Abraham descendants, land and blessing for all nations, and had renewed this promise to Isaac. A chosen heir was needed to carry it on. At Bethel (Genesis 28), when Jacob was fleeing from Esau, God stood above the ladder or stairway of his dream and repeated to him the promises made to Abraham and Isaac: land, many descendants and the blessing of all families of the earth through them. This confirmed him as the heir.

**3. Esau's disqualification.** Esau had despised his birthright and married Hittite women. Jacob, by contrast, valued the birthright and wanted the blessing, whatever the methods he used. His persistence made him fit to be the carrier of the promise.

**4. Jacob's personal qualities.** The narrative shows him as ambitious, resourceful and patient. He worked for Laban for many years to marry Leah and Rachel and to build up his family and flocks (Genesis 29-31), and he showed persistence in seeking the blessing at the Jabbok (Genesis 32), where he wrestled with a divine figure and said "I will not let you go unless you bless me". These qualities, once purified by God, were useful for the future leader of the people.

**5. The need for transformation.** The call involved discipline. Jacob had cheated his brother and was cheated by Laban. His experiences in exile and the struggle at Peniel or Penuel changed his name from Jacob to Israel (Genesis 32), a name which then became that of the whole nation. The call was thus a call to a new character and a new role.

**6. The founding of the nation.** Through his twelve sons, born in Haran and Canaan, the family became a people, and through Joseph the family went down to Egypt, preparing the Exodus. Thus Jacob's call served God's long-term plan.

**Conclusion.** Jacob was called as patriarch because God freely chose him, to continue the Abrahamic covenant and to found the people Israel, and because he, in spite of his faults, valued the promise that Esau had treated lightly.
